title: All Art is Propaganda: Reflections on Orwell and Netflix Noir
author: Jonah Raskin
content:
![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/07/Screenshot-2026-07-27-at-5.30.31-PM-680x458.png)

Finnish title screen for Deadwind - Fair Use

Born in 1942, a month after Pearl Harbor, I was unable to experience the
Thirties directly, but I experienced it vicariously in the afterglow of an
explosive era rattled by the Spanish Civil War, the anti-fascist cause, the
young Black men known as "The Scottsboro Boys" and lefty books by writers such
as Howard Fast (_Patrick Henry and the Frigate 's Keel_ ), Erika Mann (author
of  _School for Barbarians_ and the sister of the German novelist Thomas Mann)
and the songs and music of Pete Seeger, Woody Guthrie and Lead Belly with his
12-string guitar. I plead guilty to nostalgia for a time and place I never
actually knew and that can be as dangerous and addictive as any drug.

I remember my mother, a CP member, telling me about battles with landlords and
about a performance of Clifford Odets' play _Waiting for Lefty_ which brings
to life a group of New York taxi drivers and their cause. At the end of the
drama, actors on stage, along with members of the audience who cry, "Strike,
strike, strike" which made me want to go on strike. I would not do that until
1968, a good year to go on strike.

I spent much of my boyhood waiting for Lefty, or someone like him and eager to
meet striking taxi drivers. What I got was Beckett's existentialist play
_Waiting for Godot_ , and later the TV show  _Taxi._ In the 1950s I wanted to
go back to the 1930s when, my mother explained, art was supposed to advance
the class struggle and unite the exploited and the oppressed against the
exploiters and oppressors. I cheered _Rebel without a Cause,_ which was better
than no rebels at all, and _The Wild One_ which was superior to the Doris Day/
Rock Hudson kitsch movie  _Pillow Talk_.

In college I accepted and echoed George Orwell's notion that "All art is
propaganda, but not all propaganda is art." The trick, if you can call it
that, was to make something that was both artistic and propagandist and didn't
compromise one or the other. Orwell's notion landed me in trouble with the
anti-communist ex-communist professors at Columbia who hailed the Orwell who
gave the world  _Nineteen Eighty-Four_ not the Orwell who wrote  _Homage to
Catalonia_ , an imperfect work that captures the factionalism that afflicted
Spain during the civil war.

Professors such as Lionel Trilling endorsed art for art's sake or art that
gave the appearance of being apolitical such as the novels of Henry James, but
were embedded with messages about class, sex and money and about the American
bourgeoisie and the European aristocracy. In 1968, when those same professors
denounced the student strike at Columbia, I endorsed “agit-pop” as Yippie
Abbie Hoffman called it, a contemporary version of agitprop, which included
guerrilla theater actions like tossing money to the floor of the NY stock
exchange and running Pigisus, a pig for president. In the 1970s I also wrote
leaflets and pamphlets and aimed to walk the walk that journalist John Reed
had walked when he left bohemia in Greenwich Village, bounded to Russia and
chronicled the Bolshevik Revolution in  _Ten Days that Shook the World_ , a
classic of reporting about revolution.

These days with a kind of “quiet desperation,” as Henry David Thoreau would
call it, I follow my own drummer and look for both agitprop and agit pop and
for forms of cultural expression that are both artistic and propagandistic. I
look closely at film noir which I once assumed was inherently subversive, but
which now looks and feels like it has found a respectable nitch in mass media
empires like Netflix. As Jack London, the author of the dystopian novel,  _The
Iron Heel,_ observed, “Yesterday's heresy is today's orthodoxy.” Noir is now
more than ever before an industry.

Mostly, I don't find what I want and think I need. Maybe I'm looking for
subversive art in all the wrong places, much as the Miss Lonely Hearts of the
world look for love and “Mr. Goodbar” in all the wrong places. I have binged
on two Netflix cop dramas:  _Marcella,_ which is British noir, and is set in
London, and also in Belfast, a natural environment for noir; and  _Deadwind_
which takes place in and around Helsinki and in neighboring Estonia, with the
Estonians cast as the baddies.

Both  _Marcella_ and  _Deadwind_ feature fearless and seductive female cops
who break the law and who are played seductively well by two actresses (Anna
Friel in  _Marcella_ and Pihla Viitala in  _Deadwind_) who inhabit a wide
range of emotions and attitudes, from rage to tenderness and madness.

In old noir from the 1930s and 1940s, the women characters were almost always
the "femme fatale" (beautiful but deadly) who seduce and mislead male
detectives like Sam Spade (Humphrey Bogart) in  _The Maltese Falcon_ and Jeff
Bailey (Robert Mitchum) in  _Out of the Past_. In the third series of
_Marcella_ the undercover woman detective doubles as the femme fatale. In
_Deadwind_ the female cop is a step-mother and a killer who trusts no one,
takes the law into her own hands and shoots and wounds her male partner in an
attempt to rescue her kidnapped son.  _Marcella_ has far more fucking than
_Deadwind_ ;  _Deadwind_ has more violence than Marcella.

Both shows make attempts to create believable evil characters who are drug
dealers and petty criminals as well as characters who belong to wealthy,
powerful families of the sort lodged in Roman Polanski's neo-noir classic,
_Chinatown_ from 1974.  _Chinatown_ focuses on the twisted incestuous
relationship between a father (Noah Cross) and a daughter (Evelyn Cross
Mulwray), who is also the mother of their daughter. Polanki's LA is polluted,
toxic and poisonous. In  _Deadwind_ and  _Marcella_ the dramatic tension is
driven by the entanglements that exist between mothers and daughters, with
good mothers doing bad things, and bad mothers doing good things.

No one in  _Deadwind_ and in  _Marcella_ is pure and innocent. Everyone is
guilty of something, including the cops. That's what my private investigator
brother told me about the cases he handled, and not everyone, he added, was
guilty of the crime for which they were accused. In  _Chinatown,_ the
political element is water, which makes perfect sense since it’s set in
California where water is king. In  _Deadwind_ and  _Marcella_ , the political
element is corporate greed and government corruption, plus the smuggling of
drugs and arms across borders and boundaries.

It has probably been unrealistic of me to expect a mass media empire such as
Netflix to make and distribute films that are subversive. They probably
wouldn't get past internal censors. If they did, the Trump administration
would likely charge them with endorsing terrorism. It's probably more
difficult now than at any time in the past 75 years for Hollywood to make a
film like  _Chinatown_. Still now and then subversive lines surface. They're a
small consolation.

In _Marcella_ , Marcella says, "rich people don't go to jail." The film
reinforces her statement. The Maguires— a wealthy, ruthless and powerful Irish
family, headed by a matriarch, implodes— Marcella herself escapes with a child
who is the only surviving member of the criminal clan and with all their money
which she has transferred electronically from their bank account to one of her
own. Computer and phone savvy is essential in today's noir.

In  _Deadwind_ a minor character tells the detective’s daughter, who is a drug
addict, a drug dealer and a killer, that in the wake of climate change and
global warming she ought to stop eating meat and become a vegetarian. Coming
from his lips the words sound cynical. “Rich people don’t go to jail” also
sounds cynical, coming as it does from Marcella.

The two female detectives, Marcella and Sofia Karppi, both work for corrupt
police departments; so they have little or no choice but to work mostly alone,
or to be practical and expedient and to team up with tainted officers. Both
shows pay homage to the cult of the individual and offer propaganda about the
solitary and the lonely souls of the world . Marcella and Sofia are both
supercops who, like Superman, fight never ending battles. They don’t travel
faster than speeding locomotives or leap taller than skyscrapers, but they
extricate themselves from impossible traps, dark prison-like tunnels and
labyrinth-like underground passageways. You want to scream at the screen,
"Don't go there." But they go there again and again and have to be rescued.
It’s all too predictable,

I wouldn't mind a Netfix show in which the community plays the part of the
detective, solves the crimes, while the terrorists belong to a cabal that
includes the fictionalized likes of Putin, Trump, Netanyahu , the corporate
heads at Fox and a cast of thousands who cry “Strike, strike, strike” or
simply shout "Fuck You." I’ll probably keep on watching noir on Netflix hoping
against hope for something that George Orwell would have raved about.

Noir](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/07/28/all-art-is-propaganda-
